alt: Overlapping circles for family and household inside a frame for kinship. A family split across two countries is a family but not a household; a student flat-share, living alone or a commune is a household but not a family.
caption: A family need not share a home, and a household need not be a family.

alt: Left: a vertically extended family of grandmother, son, daughter-in-law and grandchildren across three generations. Right: a horizontally extended family of two married brothers and their children sharing one compound.
caption: Vertical extension adds generations; horizontal extension adds same-generation kin.

alt: Communes, living alone and foster care or children’s homes compared by what each involves and its sociological point, such as the kibbutz challenge to Murdock and Klinenberg’s Going Solo.
caption: Alternatives show child-rearing and living can be organised outside the family.

alt: Therborn compares family systems on patriarchy, marriage and fertility. He identifies five major systems and two interstitial ones, and finds patriarchy declining at different speeds, marriage diverging and fertility falling.
caption: Family systems change at different speeds, not towards one Western model.

alt: Patriarchal families give men authority, with patrilineal descent and patrilocal residence. Most so-called matriarchal examples, such as the Khasi, Minangkabau and Mosuo, are matrilineal, and mothers’ brothers may still hold authority.
caption: Matrilineal descent does not mean women rule.

alt: A scale from arranged marriage, where families lead the choice, through assisted marriage with the couple’s veto, to love marriage, where the couple choose. Forced marriage is shown apart as abuse. A note defines monogamy and serial monogamy.
caption: Arranged and love marriage differ in who chooses; forced marriage lacks consent.
